questions.question: In a normal-form game in which player $i$ has a finite set of pure strategies $S_i$, what is a mixed strategy $\sigma_i$ of player $i$?
options: A function $\sigma_i\colon S_i\to[0,1]$ whose values over $S_i$ sum to $1$
A function $\sigma_i\colon S_i\to[0,1]$ whose values over $S_i$ sum to at most $1$
A function $\sigma_i\colon S\to[0,1]$ on all profiles whose values sum to $1$
A plan that picks the pure strategy with the highest expected payoff

questions.question: Player $i$ has exactly two pure strategies, $S_i=\{H,T\}$. How many mixed strategies $\sigma_i\in\Delta S_i$ does player $i$ have?
options: Two: $H$ and $T$, each played with probability $1$
Three: $H$, $T$ and the half-half mixture of the two
One: the mixture giving $H$ and $T$ probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$ each
Infinitely many: one for each $p=\sigma_i(H)\in[0,1]$

questions.question: In a normal-form game in which player $i$ has a finite set of pure strategies $S_i$, how is a pure strategy $s_i\in S_i$ related to the set $\Delta S_i$ of mixed strategies?
options: It lies outside $\Delta S_i$, since a mixed strategy has to randomise.
It is the mixed strategy giving equal probability to all of $S_i$.
It is the mixed strategy putting probability $1$ on $s_i$ and $0$ elsewhere.
It is the mixed strategy whose support is the whole set $S_i$.

questions.question: A mixed strategy of player 2 can be read as a randomising device that player 2 uses, or as player 1's uncertainty about player 2's choice. How do the two readings compare when player 1 evaluates strategies?
options: Only the randomising-device reading allows expected payoffs to be computed.
Only the uncertainty reading is valid, since real players never randomise.
They lead to the same calculations, since player 1 maximises expected payoff either way.
They give different answers, since beliefs need not be probabilities.

questions.question: In a normal-form game in which player $i$ has a finite set of pure strategies $S_i$, the opponents' strategies are held fixed. Can a mixed strategy give player $i$ a higher expected payoff than every pure strategy of $i$?
options: Yes, since randomising adds an extra expected gain from being unpredictable.
No, since its payoff is a weighted average of payoffs of pure strategies in its support.
Yes, whenever the support contains at least two pure strategies.
No, since every mixed strategy gives exactly the average of all pure payoffs.

questions.question: Player 1 has pure strategies $T$, $M$, $B$. Which vector $(\sigma_1(T),\sigma_1(M),\sigma_1(B))$ is a mixed strategy?
Player 1 has pure strategies $T$, $M$, $B$ and uses $\sigma_1=(0.4,\,0,\,0.6)$ on $(T,M,B)$. What is the support of $\sigma_1$?

In Matching Pennies player 1 gets $1$ if the coins match and $-1$ otherwise; player 1 plays $H$ with probability $p$ and player 2 plays $H$ with probability $q$, independently. What is player 1's expected payoff when $p=0.8$ and $q=0.25$?
Player 1's pure strategy $T$ pays $4$ against $L$ and $0$ against $R$. Player 2 plays $L$ with probability $0.25$ and $R$ with probability $0.75$. What is $v_1(T,\sigma_2)$?

In Matching Pennies player 1 gets $1$ if the coins match and $-1$ otherwise; player 1 plays $H$ with probability $p$ and player 2 plays $H$ with probability $q$, independently. With $p=0.7$ and $q=0.4$, what is the probability of the profile in which player 1 plays $H$ and player 2 plays $T$?

In a normal-form game in which player $i$ has a finite set of pure strategies $S_i$, the opponents use a fixed $\sigma_{-i}$. How does $v_i(\sigma_i,\sigma_{-i})$ depend on player $i$'s own mixing probabilities?
options: It is a product of them, so mixing can raise the payoff above the best pure one.
It is strictly concave in them, so the best choice always mixes all strategies.
It is linear in them, so all mixed strategies give the same payoff.
It is linear in them, so the best mixed payoff equals the best pure payoff.

questions.question: For pure-strategy dominance only the ranking of payoffs matters. Which transformation of player 1's payoffs always preserves player 1's ranking of mixed strategies against every $\sigma_2$?
options: $w_1=f(v_1)$ for any strictly increasing $f$
$w_1=\alpha v_1+\beta$ with $\alpha>0$
$w_1=\alpha v_1+\beta$ with any $\alpha\ne0$
$w_1=v_1^2$, which keeps all payoffs nonnegative

questions.question: A firm chooses a price from the interval $S_i=[0,10]$. How is a mixed strategy over this infinite set described?
options: By a cumulative distribution function $F$, with $F(x)$ the chance of a price $\le x$
By a list of probabilities $\sigma_i(s_i)$, one for each price, summing to $1$
By one price drawn in advance, since an interval allows only pure strategies
By the expected price, since only the mean of the distribution matters

questions.question: Player 1 has $T$ and $B$, player 2 has $L$ and $R$. Player 1's payoffs are $v_1(T,L)=3$, $v_1(T,R)=0$, $v_1(B,L)=0$, $v_1(B,R)=6$. If $\sigma_1=(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2})$ on $(T,B)$ and $\sigma_2=(\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{2}{3})$ on $(L,R)$, what is $v_1(\sigma_1,\sigma_2)$?

Player 1 has pure strategies $T$, $M$, $B$; against player 2's mixture $\sigma_2$ they give expected payoffs $v_1(T,\sigma_2)=2$, $v_1(M,\sigma_2)=5$, $v_1(B,\sigma_2)=3$. What is the highest expected payoff player 1 can get with any mixed strategy?
options: $5$, by playing $M$ with probability $1$
$10$, by playing all three strategies at once
$\tfrac{10}{3}$, by mixing all three equally
$6$, by mixing $M$ and $B$ suitably

questions.question: Player 2 plays $L$ and $R$ with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$ each. Player 1's payoffs are $T$: $4$ against $L$, $0$ against $R$; $B$: $1.5$ against both. Which pure strategy maximises player 1's expected payoff with $v_1$, and with $\sqrt{v_1}$?
options: $T$ with both, since $\sqrt{\cdot}$ is strictly increasing
$B$ with both, since $B$ is never worse than $T$'s lowest payoff
$T$ with $v_1$; $B$ with $\sqrt{v_1}$
$B$ with $v_1$; $T$ with $\sqrt{v_1}$

questions.question: In Matching Pennies player 1 gets $1$ if the coins match and $-1$ otherwise; player 1 plays $H$ with probability $p$ and player 2 plays $H$ with probability $q$, independently. Two players want to "follow the same coin toss", producing $(H,H)$ and $(T,T)$ with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$ each. Why can no mixed-strategy profile $(p,q)$ produce this?
options: It can: $p=q=\tfrac{1}{2}$ gives $(H,H)$ and $(T,T)$ with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$ each.
It cannot, because a mixed strategy must give positive probability to both $H$ and $T$.
It can, provided each player uses a randomising device with the same probabilities.
Independence would need $p(1-q)=0$, which forces one of $(H,H)$ or $(T,T)$ to get probability $0$.

questions.question: Against fixed opponents, mixing never gives more than one's best pure strategy. In Matching Pennies (player 1 wins $1$ on a match, loses $1$ otherwise), why might player 1 still want to randomise?
options: Randomising raises player 1's expected payoff above that of her best pure strategy.
Randomising makes the outcome certain, since the coins then match half of the time.
Randomising is required because pure strategies are unavailable in Matching Pennies.
Randomising changes what player 2 faces: a predictable choice could be exploited by player 2.

questions.question: Player 1 has $U$, $M$, $D$ with payoffs (against $L$, against $R$): $U$: $(4,0)$, $M$: $(0,2)$, $D$: $(1,1)$. For which $\alpha$ does the mixture playing $U$ with probability $\alpha$ and $M$ with probability $1-\alpha$ strictly dominate $D$?
options: Only $\alpha=\tfrac{1}{2}$
$\tfrac{1}{4}<\alpha<\tfrac{1}{2}$
$\alpha>\tfrac{1}{4}$
Every $\alpha$ with $0<\alpha<1$

questions.question: A seller draws a price $x$ from $[0,10]$ with CDF $F(x)=x/10$. A buyer pays $x$ if $x\le6$ and walks away (payoff $0$ to the seller) if $x>6$. What is the seller's expected payoff?
